profile.story: Danielle Brooks holds the broker licence for a 40-agent independent brokerage in Nashville. Gross commission income last year was $8.5M; the brokerage's own share after splits — the company dollar — was $1.96M, and $340K of that reached the operating line. The forty agents are independent contractors she is legally barred from supervising as employees; the five people on payroll are a flat administrative function reporting to her. The brokerage's product to an agent is company-generated business, and its own routing log shows 31% of those leads never get a logged contact from anyone.

edge_cases: exactly two legitimate N/As in one pillar (S4 and S7), each with a written model-based reason — under the three-N/A threshold, so Systems is still scored on eight indicators
S4 and S7 are the deliberately arguable ones: the reasons are model constraints (independent-contractor status, delivery owned by the contractor), not 'we don't do that'
revenue field is GCI ($8.5M) while the margin, the opportunities and the constraint cost all run on company dollar — tests that the chain does not silently mix the two
customer concentration is genuinely nil while producer concentration is real — S8 scores 4 and the risk is carried on S10

intake.q2: We are an independent residential brokerage. Forty licensed agents, all independent contractors on a graduated split, and five people on payroll: two transaction coordinators, a marketing coordinator, a front-desk and licensing administrator, and a bookkeeper. The brokerage earns its money on the company side of each agent's commission, plus a per-transaction coordination fee and referral income from an affiliated title company. What we sell to an agent is leads, compliance cover, marketing support and a place to hang a licence. I hold the broker licence, so every file is legally mine whether I touched it or not.

blockNotes.b1: Danielle's stated bottleneck is agent count. Her own q4 targets are GCI per agent, lead contact rate and retention — three measures of what happens to the agents she already has. Agent count went 31 to 40 over two years while GCI per agent went $228K to $212K, which is the argument in one line. Steady on q57, not a burnout case.
blockNotes.b2: 340 consumer leads a month, all captured in Follow Up Boss, round-robined to a lead roster — and the routing log shows 31% with no logged contact by anyone, ever. Median time to contact on the rest is 4h 20m. Funnel reconciles: 4,080 routed leads × 2.4% × $11,900 = ~$1.17M of GCI, which is the 14% of the $8.5M that comes from company leads; the other 86% is agents' own business at 40 × $212,500. Pass.
blockNotes.b3: Systems tour. Follow Up Boss, Brokermint, Dotloop and QuickBooks are all real and all used, but the joins are manual — the split model is an Excel file and production reconciliation is 3.5 hours a month of retyping. Compliance queue opened: one Dotloop file carried eleven chase emails for a single missing disclosure.
blockNotes.b4: 27.7 h/wk of repetitive work against a five-person staff pool of ~200 hours — 14%, plausible, pass. The 40 agents are deliberately outside that pool: they are contractors, their hours are not the brokerage's to count, and counting them would flatter the ratio.
blockNotes.b5: Two N/As recorded here and both are model constraints, not gaps. S4: the revenue-producing population is 40 independent contractors the brokerage is legally barred from supervising, and the five staff are a flat function. S7: consumer-facing delivery consistency and capacity belong to each contractor. What the brokerage does control — file compliance and coordination — is scored on S5. Concentration on the customer axis is nil; the real concentration is three agents at 22% of GCI and it is carried on S10.

P2.note: Capture is complete — every consumer lead lands in Follow Up Boss. Response is not: the routing log shows a median 4h 20m to first logged contact and 31% with no logged contact by anyone. q24: 'Nobody at the brokerage owns the outcome.'
P2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a response inside the same half-day on every inquiry with an owner; nearly a third are never touched and the receiving agent cannot be compelled to touch them.

P3.note: A three-email brokerage nurture fires on every routed lead regardless of the agent — shown running. Beyond that, q24 puts agent-initiated second contacts at 'maybe half', and the brokerage cannot see follow-up done outside Follow Up Boss.
P3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a defined sequence used on most leads with missed follow-ups visible in the system; the sequence is three emails and the human follow-up is invisible by design.

P4.note: q25: 2.4% of routed leads become a closed side and 22% of recruiting conversations become a signed agent, both tracked by source and person in Follow Up Boss and Brokermint. No process behind either — 'that is the agent's business', and recruiting is 'me over coffee'.

S1.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs decision rights written for most areas; nothing is written, and file sign-off is a legal obligation that cannot be delegated without training the second broker — which has not been done.

S2.note: q51 four-week test: revenue does not stop — agents sell, transactions coordinate, marketing goes out. Recruiting stops, split exceptions have no approver, and broker file sign-off stops, which means nothing legally closes. Longest real absence six days, with twelve files signed from a phone.
S2.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs a named deputy; the one other licensed broker on staff has never signed a file and has never been trained to.

S3.note: Consumer-side revenue closes entirely without the owner — that part is a 4. But the brokerage's own sale is recruiting, and q30 says it is 'entirely mine'; q14 puts three personally recruited agents at 22% of GCI who 'stay because of me'.
S3.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs the team closing standard deals with the owner in on the largest 10–20%; nobody except Danielle has ever recruited an agent, and recruiting is the only sale the brokerage itself makes.

S4.note: N/A because the model cannot carry this indicator. The revenue-producing workforce is 40 independent contractors the brokerage is legally barred from supervising, directing or holding to employee-style accountability — doing so would convert them to employees and void the contractor agreements in the data room. The five people on payroll are a flat administrative function reporting directly to the owner, with one team lead over the two transaction coordinators. There is no layer of management for the indicator to describe, and scoring 0 would record a licensing constraint as a failure. The management-depth risk that does exist — no second broker trained to sign files — is scored on S2 and S10 rather than lost.
S4.why_not_higher: N/A — not scored. Rubrics v2 §5: valid only where the indicator cannot apply to the business model, with a written reason. Reason given above.

S5.note: q35: 50% documented, 40% current, 35% used in training. Compliance review and transaction coordination are the two workflows that are genuinely written down and were shown in Brokermint — but one Dotloop file opened in session carried eleven chase emails for a single missing disclosure. Recruiting and onboarding are undocumented.
S5.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs core workflows documented and current and used in training; two of ten are, and the ones that touch agents are not.

S6.note: q40 'Weekly but loose'; q39 two weekly numbers — leads routed and pendings — one of which has no owner, with no visible targets. Monthly production review is the real rhythm and it happens.
S6.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs 3–7 owned KPIs with visible targets; there are two, one is unowned, and q39 says a miss rarely triggers action because 'there is nothing to enforce against a contractor'.

S7.note: N/A because the model cannot carry this indicator. Consistency and capacity of the service delivered to the consumer sit entirely with 40 independent contractors: each sets their own standards, their own service level and their own transaction volume, and the brokerage cannot define or enforce a delivery standard over them without converting them to employees. A 20% increase in market volume lands on the agents' capacity, not the brokerage's. The portion of delivery the brokerage does control — file compliance review and transaction coordination — is documented, staffed and scored on S5, and the capacity strain in that team is carried in the L4 inventory at 13.8 h/wk.
S7.why_not_higher: N/A — not scored. Rubrics v2 §5: valid only where the indicator cannot apply to the business model, with a written reason. Reason given above.

S8.note: Production-by-agent report (Doc): the largest single transaction is 0.9% of GCI and the five largest together are 3.4%. Across 714 closed sides no consumer is material. Recorded for context: the top three producing agents are 22% of GCI — a producer concentration, not a customer one, and it is carried on S10 rather than here.
S8.why_not_higher: Top of the anchor on the customer axis, which is what v2 scores. The genuine concentration in this business is that those three agents are contractors who can leave on notice with their pipelines.

S9.note: q12: 88% of revenue is one-time transactions and 0% is contracted. Consumer re-transaction is ~4% a year on a seven-year move cycle. The only forward view is the pendings list, which covers about 45 days and converts at ~88%.
S9.why_not_higher: Anchor 2 needs some genuine repeat or contract revenue; there is no contracted revenue at all and the agents whose production makes the forecast are free to leave with it — q31 and q39 both say the forecast is a hope.

S10.note: Independent contractor agreement set — 40 agreements on one current template (Doc) — plus written vendor agreements, current licences and insurance, company-owned IP (q53). Against that, q52: the principal broker licence is the only signature that can close a file, the second licensed broker has never been trained, three agents at 22% of GCI stay on a personal relationship, and there is no continuity plan.
S10.why_not_higher: Anchor 3 needs cross-training started for key roles and a continuity plan drafted; the one role whose absence stops every closing has no trained backup, and nothing is written.

L1.why_not_higher: Anchor 4 needs every core area on a real system; recruiting — the brokerage's only sales function — runs out of the owner's phone and a spreadsheet on her laptop.

L7.note: q47: only 'Sensitive-data rules are defined' — and that is a verbal instruction not to put client financial information into a public tool. No written rules, no review, no measurement, no owner.

assessment.owner_objective: Prepare to scale — grow from 40 to 60 agents without the GCI-per-agent number continuing to fall, and get recruiting out of the owner's evenings.
assessment.owner_belief: We need more agents. Every brokerage in this market is a recruiting business and I am losing the race — two of the big franchises opened offices within a mile of us in eighteen months and they are outspending me on recruiting. If I had sixty agents instead of forty this would all take care of itself.
assessment.primary_constraint: The brokerage's only differentiated product to an agent is company-generated business, and 31% of it is never contacted by anyone — so recruiting sells a promise the operation does not keep, retention is bought back with off-schedule split concessions, and every additional agent dilutes the same leaking lead pool further.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Block 2: the routing log shows 31% of leads with no logged contact and a 4h 20m median on the rest, and the recorded consumer loss reason is 'nobody called them back fast enough'. Block 1: agent count rose from 31 to 40 while GCI per agent fell from $228K to $212K. Block 5: q52 names the lead roster itself as a key risk — 'if agents conclude the leads are not worked, the recruiting story collapses'. Block 4: the disbursement register shows eight producers on off-schedule splits granted to keep them. Four blocks; the rule requires two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$83K of expected company dollar a year from routed leads that are never contacted (routing log, Doc: 1,265 uncontacted × 2.4% close × $11,900 GCI × 23% company dollar) · ~$74K of company dollar given away in off-schedule split concessions to retain eight producers (disbursement register, Doc) · $13,500/mo of portal and paid-social spend buying leads a third of which nobody touches.
assessment.constraint_fix: Make the lead a brokerage asset with an owner rather than a gift to whoever is next on the roster: a 20-minute contact rule enforced by automatic reclaim and re-route, a visible per-agent contact-rate number, and lead-roster access earned by working the ones already given. Then recruit on a demonstrated number instead of a promise, and stop paying for retention in split points.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Turn on the reclaim rule — any routed lead with no logged contact in 20 minutes returns to the pool and re-routes. It is a configuration change in a system already in use, it costs nothing, and the contact-rate number moves inside 30 days.

opportunities.title: Contact the leads the brokerage is already paying for
opportunities.finding: The Follow Up Boss routing log (Doc) shows 4,080 consumer leads routed a year and 31% with no logged contact by anyone. Median time to contact on the rest is 4 hours 20 minutes. The brokerage spends $13,500 a month on portal and paid-social lead generation, and q27 records the consumer loss reason as 'they go to whoever called them back'. Every figure below runs on company dollar at 23%, not on GCI.
opportunities.blueprint: A 20-minute contact rule with automatic reclaim and re-route, a per-agent contact-rate number published weekly, and lead-roster access conditional on working the leads already received. None of this requires supervising a contractor: it conditions a benefit the brokerage owns, which is the only lever the model actually allows.
opportunities.replaces: A round-robin that treats a paid lead as a gift and never asks what happened to it.

opportunities.title: Replace split concessions with a written exception rule
opportunities.finding: The commission split schedule was revised in March 2024 off a real desk-cost analysis (Doc) — the economics exist and are sound. The disbursement register then shows eight producers on off-schedule splits granted case by case to retain them, worth ~$74K of company dollar last year, and company dollar per transaction on those agents is $1,910 against a $2,740 average. q28 flags no written discount rules; q32 puts 'the split exceptions I keep granting' in the owner's own top three.
opportunities.blueprint: Write the exception rule: what a producer must do to earn a split above schedule, for how long, and reviewed annually against their actual desk cost. Apply it at anniversary rather than in a retention conversation, which is why the modelled volume loss is small — an anniversary conversation with the cost math attached loses far fewer producers than a concession withdrawn mid-year. Revenue affected is company dollar ($1.96M) and the margin field is 100% because a split point is contribution with no cost beneath it; the volume-loss leg therefore carries the full company dollar of any producer who leaves, which is what makes this a narrow, disciplined move rather than a broad one.
opportunities.replaces: Retention bought one conversation at a time by the only person authorised to grant it.

opportunities.title: Work the 1,340 brokerage-owned past clients
opportunities.finding: 1,340 of the 4,200 past clients in Follow Up Boss came from brokerage-generated leads, which makes them the brokerage's to contact rather than an individual agent's. q27: no reactivation campaign has ever run and the market-update email 'nobody opens' is the entire programme. Rates below are annual re-transaction rates against a seven-year move cycle and deliberately exclude referral volume, which is where most of the real value of a worked past-client file sits.
opportunities.blueprint: Segment the 1,340 by close date and property type, run an annual home-value and equity touch that is genuinely useful rather than a market blast, and route any response to the agent who closed the original side — with the reclaim rule applying to those too. Referral outcomes are tracked separately and not counted in the range above.
opportunities.replaces: A market-update email with a 6% open rate.
